voltage.text: The difference in electrical pressure between two points, in volts (V). It is always measured between two points; a voltage "at" a point means from ground.

current.text: How much charge flows past a point each second, in amperes (A). One amp is one coulomb a second.

resistance.text: How hard a part makes it for current to flow, in ohms (Ω). Ohm's law: V = I × R.

ground.text: The point in a circuit chosen as 0 V, which every other voltage is measured from. Often the battery's − terminal or the chassis.

node.text: Every point joined by copper with no part in between: one stretch of a circuit at one voltage.

open-circuit.text: A break in the loop, such as an open switch, a cracked joint or a lifted pad. No current flows, and the full voltage appears across the gap.

short-circuit.text: A path with almost no resistance where none was meant to be, such as a solder bridge. Current is limited only by the source and the wires, and things get hot.

multimeter.text: A meter for volts, amps and ohms. Volts are measured across a part; amps through a break in the loop, with the meter in it.

ohms-law.text: For a resistor, the current is the voltage divided by the resistance: I = V ÷ R. Lamps, diodes and transistors don't keep it.

filament.text: The thin tungsten wire in a lamp, which glows when hot. Its resistance rises about tenfold from cold to lit.

series.text: Parts joined end to end on one path. They share one current; the voltage splits between them.

kirchhoff.text: The current into a junction equals the current out of it, and the voltages round any loop add up to zero.

junction.text: A point where three or more wires meet. In a semiconductor, also the boundary between p-type and n-type material.

potentiometer.text: A resistance strip with a sliding wiper: a divider you can turn. Volume and tone knobs are pots.

load.text: Whatever a source or a stage of a circuit drives: the next stage, a lamp, a motor.

impedance.text: How much a source sags under load (output impedance) or how hard a load pulls (input impedance), in ohms. For capacitors and inductors it also depends on frequency.

internal-resistance.text: The resistance inside a battery or other source, which makes its voltage sag under load.

power.text: How fast energy is used or delivered, in watts: P = V × I.

watt-hour.text: Energy: one watt for one hour, 3600 joules. Watt-hours = volts × amp-hours.

amp-hour.text: A battery's charge: one amp for one hour. Multiply by the voltage to get energy.

ampacity.text: The current a cable can carry without overheating its insulation.

fuse.text: A weak link that melts above its rated current, there to protect the wire after it.

voltage-drop.text: The volts lost along a wire or across a part: current × resistance.

signal.text: A changing voltage that carries something: sound from a pickup, a reading from a sensor. Usually a wiggle riding on a steady voltage.

frequency.text: How many times a wave repeats each second, in hertz (Hz). One over the period: a wave that repeats every 5 ms is 200 Hz.

amplitude.text: How far a wave swings from its middle to its peak. The peak to peak, bottom to top, is twice the amplitude.

alternating-current.text: Current that keeps turning round, as mains and audio signals do: AC. Current that only goes one way is direct current, DC.

clipping.text: A wave cut flat where it runs past what a stage can reach. By accident it is distortion; on purpose it is a fuzz or overdrive.

headroom.text: How far a signal can swing before it clips. Biasing a stage at half its supply gives the most headroom both ways.

capacitor.text: Two plates with an insulating gap: it stores charge, blocks a steady voltage and passes changes. Its value is in farads, usually µF or nF.

time-constant.text: τ = R × C, in seconds: how long a capacitor takes to charge 63% of the way through a resistor. About 5τ to be full.

coupling-capacitor.text: A capacitor between two stages that passes the signal and keeps their steady voltages apart.

low-pass.text: A resistor in the path and a capacitor to ground: passes low frequencies and cuts the highs above its corner. Swapped round, it is a high-pass filter.

corner-frequency.text: Where a filter lets 71% through: f = 1 ÷ (2π R C).

decoupling.text: A capacitor across a supply right by a chip, which supplies bursts of current so the voltage doesn’t dip.

inductor.text: A coil of wire. Its magnetic field resists changes in its current, so cutting the current makes a voltage spike: kickback.

diode.text: A part that conducts one way, anode to cathode, and blocks the other. The cathode is marked with a band.

forward-voltage.text: The nearly fixed voltage a conducting diode holds past its knee: 0.6–0.7 V silicon, 0.2–0.3 V germanium or Schottky, 1.8–3 V for LEDs.

led.text: A light-emitting diode. Its colour sets its forward voltage. It needs a resistor (or other limit) to set its current.

rectifier.text: Diodes that turn AC into DC: one for half-wave, four in a bridge for full-wave.

reservoir.text: The capacitor after a rectifier that fills at each peak and feeds the load between them. The sag between peaks is the ripple.

clipping-diodes.text: Two diodes back to back across a signal, which hold it to their forward voltage either way: the heart of most distortion pedals.

transistor.text: A bipolar transistor: a small current into its base lets β times as much flow from collector to emitter. NPN switches the low side; PNP the high side.

beta.text: How many times the base current a bipolar transistor lets through its collector: typically 100 to 300, varying from part to part.

saturation.text: A transistor switched fully on, dropping only a tenth of a volt or so. Drive the base with a tenth to a twentieth of the load current to get there.

mosfet.text: A transistor switched by the voltage on its insulated gate: drain, gate and source. Fully on, it is a resistance of milliohms.

threshold.text: The gate voltage at which a MOSFET starts to conduct. Fully on needs well above it; logic-level parts are fully on at 3.3 or 5 V.

relay.text: A switch worked by an electromagnet, so a small circuit can switch a separate big one.

flyback-diode.text: A diode across a coil, cathode to the supply, that carries the coil’s current when it is switched off so its kick can’t damage the switch.

gain.text: How many times bigger a stage makes a signal: out ÷ in. A common-emitter stage gives about Rc ÷ Re, inverted.

common-emitter.text: A transistor amplifier with the signal in at the base and out at the collector: gain about Rc ÷ Re, upside down.

emitter-follower.text: A transistor stage taking its output from the emitter: a gain of about 1, but a high impedance in and a low one out.

op-amp.text: An amplifier on a chip with + and − inputs and a huge gain. With negative feedback, two resistors set its gain.

negative-feedback.text: Feeding part of an amplifier’s output back to cancel some of its input, trading a large, sloppy gain for a small, exact one.

schematic.text: A drawing of a circuit showing what connects to what, laid out to be read, not to be built.

circuit-board.text: A sheet of fibreglass with copper traces for wires and pads to solder each part's legs to.

silkscreen.text: The white printing on a circuit board naming each part, R1, D1, Q1, as the schematic does.

breadboard.text: A plastic block of holes joined in rows underneath, for building a circuit without solder.

dry-joint.text: A solder joint where the solder never properly wet the lead or pad: dull, grainy, and anywhere from a few ohms to open.

half-splitting.text: Fault-finding by measuring in the middle of what's left, so each reading halves where the fault can be.
